Chapter 21: Matter as an Incomplete Record

The present state is shaped by the past; it is not the past.

Matter can carry information about its past because its present state is shaped by previous interactions. A magnet can retain remanent magnetization after a field is removed. A metal can retain mechanical history in its dislocation structure. A glass can retain features of its cooling path in a nonequilibrium configuration. None of these systems needs to replay its past. The past has altered the present.

There is a catch. The present state does not necessarily preserve enough information to reconstruct the complete sequence of events.

Memory Without a Brain

In a ferromagnetic material, domains—regions of aligned magnetic moments—can change size and orientation under an external field. When the field is removed, nonzero magnetization may remain. The information is not stored as a sentence. It is encoded in a physical configuration. Magnetic recording exploits the same principle by controlling magnetic states to represent data. The physical configuration is the memory medium.

A material’s internal state variable z(t) may evolve according to something like dz/dt = G(z, X, t), depending on its previous condition and current environment. The present is therefore influenced by history. Influence is not the same as complete retention. Two metal samples—one subjected to a single large stress cycle, another to several smaller cycles—might eventually show similar residual strain. Their present observables could agree while their histories differed. That is information loss through compression.

A useful chain is: History → Internal state → Observable response. Each arrow may discard detail. The material is a record of its past, but not necessarily a complete archive.

Figure 21.1. Many histories can lead to a similar final internal state (toy model dz/dt = −λz + αu(t)). Simulated illustrative dynamics—not a fitted material dataset.

Glass and Timescale

Glass is especially instructive because it is generally not in thermodynamic equilibrium. When a liquid cools rapidly enough, it can avoid crystallization and form a glass. Structural relaxation becomes extremely slow relative to the observation time, so the material can retain features of the conditions under which it formed. The glass transition depends strongly on cooling rate and observation timescale; it is not simply one universal sharp temperature for every glass. Below the transition, physical aging can continue: at fixed temperature, the glass may slowly relax, and its properties can change with waiting time. A glass can therefore remember, in a limited physical sense, how long it has been held under particular conditions.

How Much History Can Be Reconstructed?

If Z is a measured present state and H a possible history, the conditional Shannon entropy H(H | Z) measures remaining uncertainty about history given the measurement. Mutual information I(H; Z) = H(H) − H(H | Z) measures how much information the present retains about the past. Two questions must stay distinct: Does the material carry information about its past? Does the material carry enough information to reconstruct its past? The first can be yes while the second is no.

State Memory and Historical Memory

State memory retains information in the current configuration: magnetic orientation, residual strain, glass structure, stored charge. Historical memory retains information in a sequence of records or states: a time-stamped log, a geological layer sequence, independently retained measurements. State memory can be compact but may overwrite or compress history. Historical records can retain more detail, but only if recording, storage, and verification remain trustworthy. Neither is automatically perfect.

Statistics offers a precise cousin of this distinction. A statistic T(X) can be sufficient for a parameter θ under a specified model without preserving the entire dataset. The sample mean of independent normal observations with known variance is sufficient for the unknown mean; it does not preserve order or every detail. Physical memory often works the same way: enough for one inference, not enough for another. A magnet may retain enough to read a stored bit without retaining the exact waveform that wrote it.

Reliability Is Timed and Conditional

Physical memory is not necessarily permanent. Thermal fluctuations, mechanical stress, radiation, chemistry, fatigue, and environmental interference can degrade distinguishability. For a stored bit, reliability is not merely whether a state exists; it is whether the state remains distinguishable from competitors over the required time. The engineering question shifts from “Does the material remember?” to “How reliably, for how long, and under what conditions does it preserve distinguishable information?”

For thermally activated switching, transition rates often take an Arrhenius form Γ ∼ Γ₀ exp(−ΔE / (k_B T)). Higher barriers can improve retention and make intentional writing harder. That trade-off—easy switching versus durable retention—is shared by magnetic storage, semiconductor memory, and many biological information systems. Again, Arrhenius describes many thermally activated processes; it is not every transition.

Passive Persistence and Active Maintenance

Here a distinction that later chapters will need already appears. A crystal sitting in a metastable or equilibrium configuration need not continuously consume work merely to persist as that configuration. Passive equilibrium or metastability is different from active maintenance that depends on open-system throughput—metabolism, continuous fuel and oxidizer supply, constant repair. Landauer’s bound concerns logically irreversible erasure of information under appropriate conditions (uncertain memory bits, isothermal surroundings): the minimum heat cost associated with erasing one bit is k_B T ln 2, about 2.871 × 10⁻²¹ J at 300 K.[43] That bound is not a claim that every computation, every read, or every retained bit continuously dissipates that energy. Physical memory need not constantly pay an erasure cost simply by existing.

Identity Is Not Automatic Continuity

When we say a changing crystal is “the same crystal,” we are not usually claiming exact microscopic equality. Thermal motion alone would destroy that kind of identity every instant. What we usually mean is that a chosen description—lattice type, composition within tolerance, symmetry, defect density within bounds—remains applicable.

Let X(t) be the microscopic state and S(t) = Φ[X(t)] a deliberately coarse description. Then X₁ ≠ X₂ can coexist with Φ(X₁) ≈ Φ(X₂). That is approximate similarity under a chosen description, not physical identity of every degree of freedom. Exact equivalence under Φ requires Φ(X₁) = Φ(X₂), or else agreement of explicitly defined canonical labels.

An equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Pairwise closeness under a tolerance is not automatically an equivalence. If A is within ε of B and B within ε of C, A need not be within ε of C. A concrete counterexample: positions 0, 0.75ε, and 1.5ε. Distance(0, 0.75ε) < ε and distance(0.75ε, 1.5ε) < ε, yet distance(0, 1.5ε) = 1.5ε is not less than ε. Approximate similarity is not transitive. Using transitive closure of a tolerance relation uncritically produces drift chains that declare distant states “the same.” Prefer an explicitly defined invariant, a canonical classification, or a carefully specified approximate-similarity rule that does not pretend to be an equivalence when it is not.

Figure 21.2. Approximate similarity is not transitive. Counterexample positions 0, 0.75ε, 1.5ε—do not close under transitive chaining.

Topology language needs the same care. If one claims that a transformation preserves topology, the relevant notion is homeomorphism (or another specified topological equivalence), not an arbitrary continuous deformation that allows mergers or cuttings. Continuous motion that joins components changes topology.

Identity claims are therefore multidimensional: material, structural, functional, informational, historical. A rebuilt machine may have low material continuity and high functional continuity. A damaged crystal may retain material continuity while losing structural integrity. Continuity is a relationship across change; sameness is a more specific claim that requires a criterion.

Lattice Keeper, as Illustration Only

A practical architecture for persistent records—call it Lattice Keeper as a proposed application, not as a deployed or proven system—would separate continuity (is the state available?), integrity (does it match a trusted reference?), recoverability (can a valid state be reconstructed?), and provenance (can origin and change history be established?). A hash detects change relative to a trusted digest; it does not create that trust. A digital signature verifies under a public key that a particular key signed a message; it does not by itself establish identity of a person, permission under policy, factual truth, or authorization across time. Authorization needs key–role binding, policy, scope, time limits, revocation, and security practice. A genesis anchor remains a claimed starting point until independently evidenced. Lattice Keeper is discussed here only as a proposed application.

The Lattice Keeper’s status, stated once for the whole book. The Lattice Keeper is a proposed application, not a deployed, audited or validated system, and its Guardian policies are proposals. Its declared genesis anchor is a declaration, not an independently verified historical event: it remains claimed, unverified unless independent evidence establishes otherwise. A declared genesis record can serve as a reference point for later verification but is not independent proof of its own authenticity. Later chapters that discuss the Lattice Keeper keep this status without restating it.

Later chapters return to prediction: a present that encodes an incomplete past may still fail to forecast a future when hidden variables, rate limits, or tipping thresholds intervene (Chapter 53).

Sensitive maps and noncommuting transformations that make endpoint histories non-unique in a sharper discrete toy appear in Chapter 53.

Place to Explore

Choose one object you care about identifying across change—a mineral specimen, a software repository, a repaired instrument, or a personal archive. Write four short identity cards for it: material, structural, functional, and historical. For each card, name one measurement or document that would support the claim and one change that would falsify it. Then note one pair of states that are “close” under your tolerance but should not be declared identical by transitive chaining. The exercise is successful if your criteria become specific enough that two reasonable observers would disagree less often.

Chapter 22: Information That Survives Change

A pattern can outlast the parts that carry it.

Persistence so far has meant that a physical structure remains recognizable despite motion, thermal fluctuations, and defects. The next question is whether the same broad idea applies to information: can a pattern remain intact when the individual components carrying it change?

Yes—under specific conditions. That is the foundation of error-correcting codes, robust communication, and fault-tolerant design. The mechanisms are related to physical persistence; they are not identical to it.

A physical object persists through structural organization. An encoded message persists through redundancy and recoverability. A cryptographic record persists through verifiable evidence of history under stated trust assumptions. Three problems; three toolkits.

Repetition Coding

Transmit bit b = 1 as 111. Noise changes one bit: 111 → 101. Majority vote recovers 1. One component changed; the encoded message survived.

If each bit flips independently with probability p, majority fails when two or three flip: P_error = 3p² − 2p³. At p = 0.1, P_error = 0.028. A 10% bit-error rate becomes a 2.8% message-error rate. For odd repetition length n, P_error(n, p) = Σ_{k=(n+1)/2}^{n} C(n,k) p^k (1−p)^{n−k}. As long as p < 1/2, increasing n reduces error. The cost is more bits per original bit.

Correlation Is Not One Story

A common failure mode of intuition is to say that any correlation among errors degrades repetition coding. That is false as a blanket claim. The effect depends on the joint error distribution and on the protected function.

Extreme common-cause failure is dangerous for majority-of-three: if a disturbance flips all three bits together with probability p, majority cannot recover, and the message-error rate equals p. At p = 0.1 that is about 0.10—worse than independent noise.

Partial correlation of a particular shared-risk form—where a common factor raises each bit’s flip probability uniformly in [0, 2p]—yields an expected majority-error rate 4p²(1−p) = 0.036 at p = 0.1 (restricted to 0 ≤ p ≤ 0.5). A seeded simulation with 200,000 trials and seed 432 produced about 0.03533, consistent with that expectation.

Yet positive pairwise correlation at fixed marginal p = 0.1 can also improve majority decoding relative to independence. One joint distribution with no-error probability 0.73, each singleton-error probability 0.085, and all-three-error probability 0.015 yields majority error 0.015, which is less than the independent value 0.028. Correlation structure matters. Common-cause examples should be stated narrowly: shared flips that defeat the decoder are dangerous; correlation that reduces the probability of two-or-more errors can help.

Figure 22.1. Majority-of-three error rates under four joint models (p = 0.1). Values: 0.028, 0.10, 0.036, 0.015.

Distinguish independent noise, correlated noise, burst noise, and systematic corruption. The number of damaged components does not describe the threat by itself. Their relationship matters.

From Repetition to Hamming Codes

Repetition is inefficient. The Hamming (7,4) code uses four data bits and three parity bits. Minimum distance 3 means that in a detection-only use it can detect all double errors. In the standard single-error-correcting decoder, however, double errors are typically miscorrected: the decoder assumes a single error and can place the wrong correction. The extended (8,4) Hamming code provides a familiar SECDED distinction—single-error correction with double-error detection—precisely because the extra parity changes what the decoder can safely claim.[44] Valid codewords form a constrained subset. Noise moves a received word. Decoding finds a nearest valid codeword under the designed metric. An energy-landscape picture is a useful geometric analogy, not a thermodynamic landscape.

Shannon’s Limit, Carefully Read

For a binary symmetric channel with flip probability p, C = 1 − H₂(p), where H₂(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p). At p = 0.1, C ≈ 0.531. This is an asymptotic existence result for long block length with appropriately designed codes under the assumed channel model. It is not a construction for finite n, and it is not a promise that every practical code achieves the bound. Reliable preservation is not free. It requires resources, structure, and an error model the protection can handle.

Integrity, Backup, and Provenance

A hash detects; it does not repair. Compare a trusted digest of original data with the digest of a damaged copy: a single flipped bit changes the digest, and the integrity check fails. Restoring from a backup can recover bytes; a same-process copy of the original is a trivial recovery assumption, not a demonstration of provenance. A code reconstructs within limits; it does not establish who created the original or whether creation was authorized. Later chapters return to Merkle inclusion proofs and independent checkpoints: membership in a committed tree is still not accuracy, authorization, or completeness (Chapter 64).

Figure 22.2. Detection, recovery, and provenance are distinct mechanisms.

Four distinct questions: continuity—is the state still available?; integrity—does it match its trusted reference?; recoverability—can a valid state be reconstructed?; provenance—can origin and change history be established? Preserve evidence of change, not merely the appearance of an unchanged state.

Pattern Versus Components

In Conway’s Game of Life, a glider changes its exact occupied cells every generation while remaining a recognizable moving pattern. Formally one may write X(t₁) ≠ X(t₂) while P(t₁) ≅ P(t₂), where X is microscopic configuration, P is recognized pattern, and ≅ means equivalence under a specified recognition rule and allowed transformations. The recognition rule must be stated. Without it, “same pattern” is a slogan.

Physical Cost of Forgetting

Information is represented by physical states. Retention depends on the stability of those states; recovery depends on the structure of the encoding; logically irreversible erasure has a minimum thermodynamic cost under Landauer’s conditions. Retention, recovery, and erasure are not the same operation. The Landauer bound is not a prediction of the power consumption of a modern computer chip. It bounds ideal irreversible erasure in the appropriate thermodynamic setting. Keeping a bit is not automatically paying that cost each tick of the clock.

Place to Explore

Implement majority-of-three decoding for independent bit flips at p = 0.1 with a fixed seed, and compare the empirical error rate to 3p² − 2p³ = 0.028. Then construct one joint distribution with the same marginal flip probability in which majority error is higher than 0.028 (shared all-flip), and one in which it is lower (the 0.015 triple-error example above, or any other joint you can specify). Report the joints explicitly. The point is not to find a universal law of correlation; it is to stop saying “correlation” when you mean one particular failure mode.

Chapter 23: Measurement, Provenance, and Authenticity

A record can be authentic and still be wrong.

Physical structure can persist while interpretable history is lost. This chapter develops provenance and measurement: how a reading is made, corrected, and trusted—and what those steps do not prove.

Four Separate Questions

When examining a record, keep four questions distinct:

1. Origin — where did the record come from? 2. Integrity — has it changed since creation? 3. Accuracy — does it correctly represent what it claims to measure? 4. Interpretation — does the evidence justify the conclusion drawn?

A digital signature can help show that a particular key signed a particular byte string. It does not show that the key holder was truthful, that the sensor was calibrated, or that the conclusion is warranted.

The Measurement Chain

An observation typically passes through

Reality → interaction → sensor → signal → processing → record → interpretation.

Every stage can add uncertainty. A thermometer that prints 25.4 °C has not automatically reported the exact thermodynamic temperature. A more honest report might be 25.4 ± 0.3 °C, but only when the ±0.3 is justified by calibration, resolution, repeatability, environment, and procedure. Decimal places are not accuracy. “±0.3” must say whether it denotes a standard uncertainty, a stated coverage interval, or something else under stated calibration conditions. The BIPM/JCGM Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM) is the standard reference for stating and combining measurement uncertainties.[45]

Calibration and Correction

A simple instrument model is

y = a + b T ,

with reading y and reference temperature T. When b ≠ 0 and the calibration is known over a stated range,

T_corrected = (y − a)/b .

The correction is only as trustworthy as the estimates of a and b and the covariance structure used for uncertainty propagation (again following a GUM-style treatment when covariances are modeled). A synthetic demonstration with deliberately planted offset and scale recovers the planted truth when those parameters are treated as known; that is a teaching plot, not validation of a real meter.

Figure 23.1. Synthetic thermometer with planted offset and scale error, then correction using the known parameters. Demonstration—not a validated field calibration.

Traceability means a documented chain of comparisons to recognized standards, each with stated uncertainty. Calibration today does not prove permanent accuracy tomorrow.

Provenance and Copies

Provenance is the documented history of an object or record: who collected it, when, with what instrument, under what storage and processing steps, with which software versions. Multiple identical copies of a wrong reading are still wrong. Independent evidence is not the same as repeated agreement on a shared corrupted source. Common calibration bias and shared upstream data are common-mode risks.

Bayes and Conditional Independence

Bayes’ theorem updates beliefs given evidence. Marginal likelihood ratios from several observations may be multiplied only under conditional independence given both the hypothesis and its alternative; conditionally updated likelihood ratios can incorporate dependence without that product assumption. Treating “more agreeing reports” as automatic confirmation without that structure confuses correlation with independent information. Consensus counts are not a generic substitute for a likelihood model, and they are not a proof of scientific truth.

Authenticity Is Not Accuracy

An authentic, integrity-checked record can still be inaccurate. Integrity tools answer whether bytes match a commitment; accuracy tools answer whether the measurement chain was adequate. Interpretation asks whether the conclusion follows. Collapsing these into one “verified” badge is how systems overclaim.

Thesis

Persistence of a record is not persistence of a fact. Origin, integrity, accuracy, and interpretation demand different methods. Calibration and provenance strengthen measurement claims only within their stated scope; authentic wrongness remains possible.

Place to Explore

Take one measurement you trust this week (a kitchen scale, a weather app, a lab notebook entry). Write one sentence for each of the four questions—origin, integrity, accuracy, interpretation—naming what evidence you actually have, and one failure mode that would leave a signature or hash still “valid” while the conclusion is wrong.

Connections

Chapter 21 treated matter as an incomplete record of its past. Chapter 22 treated hashes and signatures as integrity tools, not as certificates of origin or accuracy.

Chapter 24: Clocks, Causality, and Sampling

A timestamp and a sample are both incomplete stories about what happened between marks.

Here the questions are temporal order without a shared perfect clock, and what regular sampling can and cannot recover. Relativity enters only as a scoped reminder that spacelike separation is not a license for causal signalling—not as a claim that distributed clocks are the same physics.

Physical Clocks Drift

A fractional rate offset of 10 ppm accumulates about 0.864 s per 86400 s day if the rate is constant. Two clocks each within ±10 ppm of a reference can differ by up to about 20 ppm relative to each other. Synchronization protocols reduce but do not erase uncertainty from asymmetric delays, reference quality, and local oscillators.

Logical Time and Happened-Before

Lamport logical clocks increment on local events; a send carries the clock; a receive sets the local clock to max(local, message) + 1.[46] If event A happened-before B, then C(A) < C(B). The converse is false: C(A) < C(B) does not imply that A happened-before B; concurrent events can have unequal readings. Equal clock readings likewise do not establish physical simultaneity. Vector clocks can refine concurrency detection when properly maintained; they are optional machinery, not assumed here. Logical clocks order events; they do not measure elapsed seconds.

Timestamps with Uncertainty

Physical interval order is trustworthy only when intervals remain disjoint after stated timing bounds. Overlapping uncertainty intervals leave order unresolved. Perfect synchronization is not an asymptotic free gift.

Spacelike Separation Is Not a Messaging Shortcut

In special relativity, with the metric signature s² = c² dt² − dx² − dy² − dz² in an inertial chart, a spacelike separation has frame-dependent time order and admits no subluminal or lightlike causal link between the events.[47] Timelike order is preserved for orthochronous observers. Distributed-system clock analogies should not be confused with that geometry.

Sampling and Aliasing

Uniform samples with interval Δt have sampling frequency f_s = 1/Δt. Shannon’s sampling theorem reconstructs a strictly band-limited signal from regular samples when f_s > 2 f_max under ideal infinite-precision conditions;[48] equality at the Nyquist rate is an edge case with phase sensitivity. Finite windows, noise, quantization, and irregular timing all weaken the guarantee. Anti-alias filtering belongs before the converter.

At f_s = 10 Hz, the continuous signals cos(2π·4·t) and cos(2π·6·t) share identical samples at t = n/10 for integer n, because cos is even and 6 ≡ −4 (mod 10). The continuous curves differ; the discrete records do not. The corresponding sines are opposite at those instants (except zeros), not identical. Nyquist frequency here is 5 Hz; 6 Hz lies above it and aliases to 4 Hz.

Figure 24.1. cos(2π·4t) and cos(2π·6t) with identical samples at f_s=10 Hz. Continuous curves differ; discrete records match. Ideal toy—not a measured ADC capture.

Figure 24.2. Schematic Lamport clock update on send/receive: happened-before implies smaller clock; smaller clock does not imply happened-before. Logical order—not elapsed seconds.

Frames and Proper Time (Scoped)

Classical Galilean change of frame, x′ = x − v t and u′ = u − v, applies in its Newtonian domain. For a timelike worldline at constant speed v relative to an inertial frame, proper time along that worldline satisfies

dτ = dt √(1 − v²/c²)

under the usual special-relativistic assumptions (inertial comparison; events on the same worldline).[47] This chapter uses the (+,−,−,−) interval convention already stated above; an opposite overall sign elsewhere is a convention choice, not a different physical geometry. The formula is not a twin-paradox narrative and does not supply a single global clock for distributed systems.

Thesis

Order and continuity are easy to overclaim from timestamps and samples. Logical clocks track causality under stated rules; physical clocks carry uncertainty; band-limited sampling theorems do not resurrect every history from sparse marks.

Place to Explore

At f_s = 10 Hz, evaluate cos(2π·4·n/10) and cos(2π·6·n/10) for n = 0…9 and report the maximum absolute difference. Separately, sketch two concurrent events that receive different Lamport times and explain why that does not contradict the happened-before rule.

Connections

Chapter 2 treated observation windows; Chapter 23 treated measurement uncertainty.

Chapter 25: Evidence Lifecycle and Observer Disagreement

The object can fail while the record survives—or the reverse.

This chapter separates system survival from evidence survival and shows how disagreeing observers can be fused under stated noise models without crowning consensus as truth.

From Event to Verifiable Record

A useful lifecycle is

X → O → R → A → V

(event or state → observation → record → archive → verification). Integrity, availability, interpretability, and verifiability are distinct properties; metadata, format, access, and keys age differently from raw bits. Retention and access policy are engineering choices for a given project. A file checksum verifies that bytes match a trusted reference; a signature or root can authenticate a commitment under a declared trust boundary, but neither establishes event truth or accuracy of the claim—even when the trust boundary is accepted. That distinction between integrity tools and accuracy was already drawn for signatures in earlier chapters.

Figure 25.1. Schematic evidence lifecycle X→O→R→A→V with separate failure marks for object vs record. Conceptual diagram—not a deployed archive audit.

Observers Who Disagree

Write Y_i = h_i(X) + e_i. Disagreement can mean different measurands or models, different noise, or different interpretation—not automatic subjectivity of truth. For independent Gaussian unbiased measurements of the same scalar quantity with known variances σ_i², the inverse-variance combination is

x̂ = Σ (y_i / σ_i²) / Σ (1/σ_i²), σ̂ = 1 / √(Σ 1/σ_i²).[45]

A two-observer standardized difference

z = |y₁ − y₂| / √(Var(y₁ − y₂))

uses the square root of the difference variance in the denominator. Under independence that variance is σ₁² + σ₂²; with known covariance it is σ₁² + σ₂² − 2 Cov(y₁, y₂). Unknown shared bias cannot be averaged away: if both readings carry the same additive bias b, the fused x̂ shifts by b as well (for example, unbiased fuse of 10 and 11 with σ = 1 and 3 gives 10.1; adding +2 to both yields 12.1). When a known nonsingular positive-definite covariance Σ is available, the GLS scalar combiner is (1ᵀ Σ⁻¹ y) / (1ᵀ Σ⁻¹ 1). Consensus among observers remains agreement, not automatic ground truth—Chapter 64 made that point for quorums.

Figure 25.2. Inverse-variance fuse of two toy Gaussian observers (σ=1 and σ=3) vs each alone. Computed under declared model—not empirical lab data.

Chapter 28 asks what happens before and after fusion: how conflicting archives preserve both originals and document an evidence-based correction.

Thesis

Evidence can outlive or die independently of the system it describes. Fusion under a noise model reduces variance only under its assumptions. Disagreement is a fact about observations; it neither dissolves measurement nor crowns majority as reality.

Place to Explore

Take y₁ = 10.0, σ₁ = 1 and y₂ = 11.0, σ₂ = 3. Compute x̂ and σ̂ under inverse-variance weighting. Then add a shared bias of +2 to both readings and recompute—confirm the fuse becomes 12.1 and does not remove the bias.

Connections

Chapter 22 treated hashes and backups; Chapter 23 treated measurement chains; Chapter 64 treated agreement versus truth.

Chapter 26: Reconstruction, Bottlenecks, and Observability

Consistency with surviving fragments is not uniqueness of the past.

Here the focus is inverse problems, what context must survive for meaning, and when a linear model’s state is observable from outputs.

Choosing Among Consistent Reconstructions

An observation model Y = F(X, θ) need not determine a unique X. When many X fit the data, a regularized reconstruction

argmin_X ‖Y − F(X, θ)‖² + λ R(X), λ ≥ 0,

uses a penalty R (not the lineage reproduction number of Chapter 43) to choose among them.[49] Existence, uniqueness, and sensitivity remain separate questions; the penalty does not recover historical truth by itself. Identifiable inverses with a unique solution do not require such a choice. Example: x₁ + x₂ = 10 with integers x_i ∈ {0,…,10} has eleven solutions; with nonnegative reals the solution set is an infinite segment. Minimum Euclidean norm on the exact feasible set picks (5, 5), which is a convention, not proof of the past. That hard feasible projection is distinct from a soft residual-plus-penalty problem at finite λ > 0, which need not land exactly on the constraint.

Figure 26.1. Feasible set x₁+x₂=10, x_i≥0, with min-‖·‖₂ point (5,5) and a Tikhonov-style preference toward a prior (8,2). Computed toy—not a recovered archive.

Lossy metadata—units, time base, calibration version—can make intact raw samples uninterpretable. Not every bit has equal reconstruction value for a stated task; cost–quality tradeoffs are task-relative. Expected loss E[L(X, g(Z))] under Cost(Z) ≤ B is a conceptual rate–distortion sketch, not Shannon’s theorem under full assumptions.

Linear Observability

For a known continuous-time LTI model ẋ = A x, y = C x of finite dimension n, the observability matrix

O = [C; CA; …; CA^{n−1}]

has full rank n if and only if the state is observable from the output over an interval (exact, noiseless theory).[50] Observability is not “seen from one sample,” not automatic for nonlinear models, and not parameter identifiability of unknown θ. Noise, poor conditioning, short windows, and aliasing can impair practice even when rank(O) = n. Detectability is weaker: for continuous-time LTI, every unobservable mode must be strictly stable (Re(λ) < 0); modes with Re(λ) = 0 or Re(λ) > 0 must be observable.

Example (computed): A = [[0, 1], [0, 0]], C = [1, 0] yields rank(O) = 2 (observable double integrator position). A = [[0, 0], [0, 0]], C = [1, 0] yields rank 1 (unobservable free second state).

Figure 26.2. Singular values of O for the observable double-integrator pair vs an unobservable pair. Rank/SVD of toy matrices—not a plant identification.

Thesis

Reconstruction chooses among stories consistent with fragments. Observability is a property of a known linear model and its sensors, not a warrant that the world has been seen whole. Context lost can be as fatal as bits lost.

Place to Explore

Build O for A = [[0, 1], [0, −0.5]], C = [1, 0] and report rank and the two singular values. Then change C to [0, 1] and repeat—what changed?

Chapter 21 already noted many histories per endpoint; Chapter 23 treated calibration.

Chapter 27: Silent Gaps and the Expected Record

An intact archive can still be missing the event that matters.

The new source adds a narrower question: what independent expectation lets an observer notice that something never entered the record?

Integrity Is Not Completeness

Integrity asks whether retained items changed. Completeness asks whether every item within a declared scope was captured and retained. A collection can pass every integrity check while omitting events. A completeness ratio, observed required records divided by expected required records, is meaningful only when the denominator is defined and estimated independently. An archive that defines its expected universe as whatever it happens to contain will always certify itself.

Sequential identifiers help only within their own assignment process. The sequence 1001, 1002, 1003, 1005, 1006 exposes a missing 1004. It cannot reveal an event never assigned a number, a lost record after 1006, or a numbering process that was itself restarted. Compare against independent sources such as transaction counters, external receipts, sensor logs, physical inventory, or periodic checkpoints. Each source must also have its own scope and failure modes.

Missingness has structure.[51] In Rubin’s terms, data are missing completely at random when missingness is unrelated to observed and unobserved values; missing at random when it depends only on observed information; and missing not at random when it depends on unobserved values or processes. Failures, embarrassing decisions, or outages that disabled the recorder can create the last pattern. The label states an assumption; it is not automatically testable from the retained records alone.

When Silence Is Evidence

Absence is evidence only relative to a detection model. Suppose an event of interest has prior probability π. If it occurs, a working recorder retains it with probability p_d. Assume no false records. Then

P(event | no record) = π(1−p_d) / [π(1−p_d) + 1−π].

With π=0.5, p_d=0.9 gives 1/11≈0.091; p_d=0.5 gives 1/3; and p_d=0 leaves 0.5. Silence from a recorder that could not detect the event is no evidence. The calculation also requires knowing that the recorder was operating and that retention did not depend on the event’s content.

Figure 27.1. Left: two partially overlapping event sources with n₁=60, n₂=50 and m=30 shared records; under closure, independence and equal capture probabilities the Lincoln–Petersen estimate is 100, implying 20 events seen by neither. Right: posterior probability that an event occurred despite no record, as recorder detection probability changes. Constructed numbers, not an audited archive.

Two overlapping collections can sometimes estimate what neither captured. If source A records n₁ events, source B records n₂, and m appear in both, the Lincoln–Petersen estimate is N̂=n₁n₂/m. Chapman’s small-sample form is (n₁+1)(n₂+1)/(m+1)−1.[52] For n₁=60, n₂=50 and m=30, these give 100 and about 99.35. The two sources jointly saw 80 distinct events, so the simple estimate implies 20 unseen.

These estimators assume a closed population, correctly matched records, and independent capture with comparable catchability. If both systems consume the same feed or miss the same difficult cases, overlap rises and the total tends to be underestimated. Different event types may need stratification. The method reveals a possible gap; it does not identify the missing events.

Keys, Clocks, and Time Fields

A key succession record can contain predecessor and successor public keys, transition time, authority, and supporting evidence. A transition signed by both keys establishes a cryptographic relationship only if the predecessor was still controlled by the rightful holder. If K₀ may have been compromised at an uncertain time, signatures after the earliest plausible compromise need independent timestamping, checkpoints, revocation evidence, or custody records. Chapter 28’s rule remains: a new signature attests later; it does not retroactively validate the old origin.

An event can occur at 10:00, be recorded at 10:03, reach a server at 10:07, and be verified at 10:15. Store event, record, receipt, and verification times separately, with clock source, synchronization context, uncertainty, and any causal order. Chapter 24 covers Lamport and vector clocks: a smaller Lamport value does not prove causation.

Network synchronization illustrates why precision is not accuracy.[53] Let a client send at T₁=100.000 s by its clock, the server receive at T₂=100.060 s and reply at T₃=100.061 s by the server clock, and the client receive at T₄=100.041 s. The usual offset estimate is θ=[(T₂−T₁)+(T₃−T₄)]/2=0.040 s. Round-trip network delay is δ=(T₄−T₁)−(T₃−T₂)=0.040 s. If clock rates are constant during the exchange and one-way delays are nonnegative but unknown, the actual offset lies in θ±δ/2: from 0.020 to 0.060 s. The midpoint is exact only if the paths are symmetric.

Thesis

Preserve the expected universe, recorder availability, exclusions, and known gaps along with the records themselves. A durable history should make omissions discoverable rather than presenting tidy silence as fact.

Finally, change T₄ in the synchronization example to 100.081 s and derive the new offset estimate and its interval.

Chapter 28: Archives That Can Disagree and Correct Themselves

Keep the disagreement visible until the investigation earns its conclusion.

Two internally consistent archives can tell different stories. Now preserve the competing accounts, their origins, and the investigation that changes their standing. Reconciliation needs evidence, not silent replacement.

Preserve Before Combining

Suppose A records 10.2 ± 0.2 and B records 11.0 ± 0.2, where the uncertainties are one-standard-deviation estimates for independent, approximately Gaussian errors in measurements of the same quantity under comparable conditions. Chapter 25’s standardized difference gives z = 0.8/√(0.2² + 0.2²) ≈ 2.83. That is a reason to investigate the stated noise model, calibration, and collection conditions—not a verdict that A or B is false. A different measurand, clock error, shared bias, or selection process can invalidate a naive comparison. Averaging first can conceal the very discrepancy that needs explanation.

Retain both originals, their custody and transformation histories, the exact conflict, and the comparison method. Add an investigation record stating whether a successor corrects a calibration error, measures different conditions, supplies genuinely new evidence, or merely reinterprets existing material. Evidence succession and interpretation succession are not the same. Neither the most recent file nor the most numerous copies automatically deserve authority.

Figure 28.1. Conflicting originals feed an investigation and a revisable current assessment. A later observation is distinct from a later interpretation. Schematic evidence relationships—not a verified archive.

A Minimum Record for a Challengeable Claim

The source proposes H = (C, E, P, M, U, T): claim, evidence, provenance, method, uncertainty, and transformation/assessment history. This is a checklist, not an archival standard or numerical confidence formula. Ask of each field whether its scope and source are identifiable and its limitations examinable. An unknown origin should be marked unknown rather than reconstructed from an attractive narrative.

Keep claim status separate from artifact status. A digest match, a successful signature check, a corroborating observation, and an unresolved factual question can coexist. “Locally checked” must name the checks; “independently assessed” must identify both examiner and independence boundary. These structures describe a possible architecture, not evidence that one has been deployed or audited.

Cryptographic Evidence Ages Too

Chapter 23 distinguished provenance from intact bytes. Long-term signatures add a further difficulty: an old signature can still satisfy its verification algorithm after the algorithm or key is no longer trusted. Preserve the original message and signature, public verification material, algorithm and parameters, trust/authorization evidence, assessment time, and the historical verification procedure and result when available. Public verification material is not a reason to expose private signing keys.

A migration can commit to that package and record a new signature under a newer scheme. The new signature establishes a later attestation under its own assumptions; it cannot retroactively repair a missing timestamp, compromised key, or fabricated origin. Historical timestamps, certificate status, and custody may matter. Algorithm agility must not launder uncertainty into a fresh “valid” badge.

Disclosure, Correction, and Present Authority

A malicious archive can hash a fabrication correctly. Its safeguards therefore need independent witnesses or references, scope evidence about excluded records, and separation of administrative control—not just more copies. The same threat analysis must consider confidentiality. A public hash of a predictable sensitive value is not necessarily hiding: someone can guess candidates and compare their hashes. Purpose-built commitments with appropriate randomness, selective-disclosure credentials, Merkle proofs, and zero-knowledge techniques make different promises; none proves an unmeasured real-world input truthful merely by proving a mathematical statement about it.

Disclose enough to evaluate the stated claim and label what has been withheld. An inclusion proof answers membership relative to a root, not whether omitted records would change the conclusion. A threshold proof does not establish that the threshold is fair or that the measurement is accurate. Restricted originals and public audit evidence can have different retention schedules. Metadata and commitments can themselves expose identities or relationships; minimization and re-identification analysis apply to them too.

Correction should link the original claim, reason, supporting evidence, responsible authority, effective time, revised claim, and residual uncertainty. A current view can prominently show the correction while the permitted historical trail remains distinguishable. This is not a command to retain sensitive originals forever: Chapter 34’s lawful deletion and access constraints still apply, including to the audit trail itself. A deletion log records an authorized action; it is not automatic proof that every uncontrolled copy has vanished.

Authenticity, accuracy, relevance, and current authority are separate. A genuine old policy can be obsolete. Check issuer, scope, governing basis, applicable period, and succession before applying it. Survival grants evidence a hearing, not perpetual authority.

Distinguish the custodian who protects a record, the interpreter who assesses it, the certifier who attests to a specified property, and the governance authority who controls permissions. One institution may hold several roles; custody of the only surviving copy still does not make its interpretation correct. Privacy or lawful restriction can limit access without licensing concealed alteration; even the audit trail needs proportionate protection.

Thesis

A trustworthy archive preserves the possibility of challenge: competing accounts, changing verification assumptions, proportionate disclosure, justified correction, and explicit authority boundaries. Its current assessment can change without pretending that its history never did.

Then create a third record documenting a hypothetical calibration correction, leaving both originals untouched. Draw the predecessor links and mark separately what is intact, what is authorized, and what is factually unresolved. Chapter 29: What Institutions Select and Channels Distort

A record can survive every checksum and still lose the qualification that made it honest.

Institutions reward some outcomes and discourage others; communication selects and transforms what remains. Integrity engineering must examine the reporting boundary, not only stored bytes.

When the Denominator Disappears

Consider a constructed month with 90 successful operations and 10 failures. The success fraction over all operations is 90/100 = 90%. If eight failures are omitted while every success is reported, the displayed fraction becomes 90/92 ≈ 97.83%. No operation improved; the denominator changed. Comparing the two percentages as operational progress would confuse reporting selection with performance.

This illustrates Goodhart’s law: a target can change behavior until its metric ceases to represent its intended object. It is a warning, not a theorem that every target fails. Dashboards cannot repair reporting that punishes disclosure. Reconcile attempted operations with reported outcomes; distinguish failure, missing report, and excluded scope.

Figure 29.1. The same 90 successes and 10 failures produce a 90% complete-record rate or a 97.83% selective-report rate when eight failures disappear. Constructed arithmetic—not evidence about a real institution.

Preserve relevant, lawful negative findings, failed projects, conflicts of interest, and dissent. Protect correction channels, separate assessment from incentives to appear successful, and explain exclusions. These fallible safeguards do not guarantee candor. Chapter 34’s privacy and retention limits still govern what may be kept.

Selection Favors Transmission, Not Necessarily Truth

Chapter 43’s selection models concern reproduction under a specified rule. Applied as an analogy to records, a message’s transmission weight might reflect memorability, institutional preference, cost, or access to a gatekeeper. None is automatically a measure of accuracy. A widely repeated conclusion can descend from one original observation; a poorly circulated correction can have stronger evidence.

Trace dependencies before counting confirmations (Chapter 65): repetition is not independent measurement. Preserve strong contrary evidence with its methods and limitations, without manufacturing false balance between unsupported opinions. An archive of successful projects alone cannot estimate all attempted projects’ failure rate without information about the missing population.

Endpoint Error Is Not Every Error Along the Way

For a deliberately narrow channel model, let each of n independent transmissions flip a single bit with the same symmetric probability p. The endpoint differs from the original exactly when the number of flips is odd. If q_n is that probability, then q_(n+1) = p + (1−2p)q_n, with q_0 = 0. Consequently,

q_n = [1 − (1−2p)^n]/2.

The probability of at least one flip anywhere is instead 1 − (1−p)^n. Two flips restore the original bit but do not mean the transmission history was error-free. At p=0.1 and n=10 these probabilities are about 0.4463 and 0.6513, respectively. The approximation q_n ≈ np is useful only for sufficiently small cumulative error; at these values np=1 is already poor. For 0<p<0.5, endpoint error tends toward 1/2 as n grows, not toward certainty.

Figure 29.2. Endpoint disagreement and any-flip history have different probabilities in an independent symmetric bit channel with p=0.1. Analytic illustration; neither curve measures loss of meaning in human communication.

The model does not describe translation, quotation, editorial selection, or adversarial distortion merely by renaming p. A statement such as “effective in the tested configuration” can become “effective” without any bit error. Preserve transformation inputs and outputs, tool or method versions, omitted scope, uncertainty, and significant ambiguities. Chapter 22 supplies the coding example; repeating its majority vote would not solve semantic loss or a wrong reference.

Correction Must Travel Too

A correction linked only in a secluded archive may never reach the audience that received the original. Map the dissemination path and attach a clearly scoped correction where practicable, without unnecessarily amplifying harmful content. The source’s epidemic analogy describes sharing, not truth: stopping transmission need not mean changing belief; renewed attention need not mean new evidence. Its equations are not an empirically fitted account of misinformation here.

Distinguish suspected adversarial manipulation from demonstrated intent. A genuine signed statement can be replayed outside its period of authority or stripped of context. Check freshness and applicable scope separately from signature validity. A custody handoff can record sender, recipient, item identity, release, receipt, and checks; a missing receipt is a documented gap, not automatic proof of tampering. Conversely, matching bytes do not establish continuous possession. Existing authentication, quorum, and custody arguments remain in Chapters 9, 15, 23, 28, 64, 65, 79 and 80.

Thesis

Persistence depends on what enters the record, what survives transformation, and whether correction reaches its users. A clean endpoint is not a complete history; a popular message is not independent corroboration.

Place to Explore

Using the fictional 90-success/10-failure month, calculate the displayed rate after eight failures are omitted. Specify a reconciliation record that would reveal the omission without publishing personal details. Then enumerate the four two-hop flip histories at p=0.1: compare the probability of any flip with endpoint disagreement. Finally, shorten “effective only in the tested configuration” to a headline and explicitly record the qualification your headline must retain.

Chapter 30: Memory Is Not Truth: Custodians, Correction, and Long Horizons

A claim can survive a thousand years without becoming one year truer.

Principles 689–703 cover shared knowledge, memory and truth, intergenerational learning, the limits of a universal archive, future custodians, institutional memory, knowledge under disruption, truth, authority and trust, self-correction, the present generation’s responsibility, long-term responsibility, the seven-hundredth principle, completion and continuation, an unfinished legacy, and the next horizon. Much of this develops earlier chapters. This chapter adds calculations for the information lost along a chain of transmission, a weakest-link capacity, the steady level of uncorrected error, and the scale of long-horizon discounting.

Agreement Is Not Independence

The source’s formula Var(X̄)=(σ²/N)[1+(N−1)ρ] for correlated observers is correct. Chapter 50 drew its consequence: the effective number of independent observers never exceeds 1/ρ. The source’s failure mode, many people repeating one source, is the extreme case ρ→1, where a thousand repetitions carry the evidential weight of one.

Each Step From Event to Claim Can Only Lose Information

The source traces a claim along X→O→R→I→C: event, observation, record, interpretation and claim. It then states the data processing inequality for a chain X→Y→Z, I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y).[54] A worked case shows how fast losses compound. Suppose a yes-or-no fact is passed through two independent steps, each of which flips it with probability 0.1. One step leaves about 0.53 bits of the original 1 bit. Two steps act like a single flip probability of 0.18 and leave about 0.32 bits. No later analysis can recover the difference without new evidence from outside the chain. This is the precise version of the source’s point that a statement’s survival is not proof of its truth, and it is why the source’s status labels (observed, recorded, inferred, reconstructed, corroborated, unknown) should travel with a claim (Chapter 26). The source also says a universal archive is impossible. Physical limits, incomplete observation and ethical limits on retention all apply, and the useful response is to declare what an archive contains, how it was assembled and what it excludes.

Figure 30.1. Left: information about a one-bit fact after k independent steps, each flipping it with probability 0.1 or 0.05; information never increases along the chain. Right: accumulated error eₜ₊₁=eₜ−qeₜ+c with c=5 new errors per period, for detection fractions q=0.25 (steady level 20) and q=0.05 (steady level 100). Illustrative models.

Institutional Memory Has a Weakest Link

The source’s institutional memory MI=(D,K,S,P,A) — data, knowledge, skills, procedures and authority — comes with a bottleneck model, C_I=min(D,K,S,P,A), which it labels illustrative. The labelling matters. If those components are scored 0.9, 0.8, 0.3, 0.9 and 0.85, their average is 0.75 but the bottleneck is 0.3. A report on document volume, the source’s failure mode, would see the 0.9 and miss the 0.3. A minimum is right when every component is necessary and cannot substitute for another. Where training can partly make up for missing documents, a minimum is too pessimistic. The choice of aggregation is a claim about the institution, as Chapter 54 argued for viability floors. For knowledge under disruption, the source’s R=1−(1−r)^N for N independent copies, with its warning that shared infrastructure invalidates it, is Chapter 60’s result. With r=0.6 and five copies, survival is about 0.990. A 5% hazard that destroys all copies together, such as a common grid, provider or credential, lowers it to about 0.940.

Correction Must Outpace New Error

The source’s error accounting eₜ₊₁=eₜ−dₜ+cₜ is conceptual, as it says. Giving it one rule shows why its emphasis on protected dissent is quantitative and not only moral. If a fraction q of existing errors is found and removed each period and c new errors arrive, the error stock settles at c/q. With c=5 and q=0.25 that is 20. If people who report mistakes are punished and detection falls to q=0.05, the same institution settles at 100: five times the error, with nothing else changed. The source keeps truth, authority and trust distinct: lawful authority can make an inaccurate claim, an accurate observer may have no authority, and a popular institution can be wrong. Its trust function TP=f(E,V,A,C) is a framework, not a measurement, and Chapter 86 treated legitimacy that has to be earned.

Long Horizons: Discounting, Options, and Milestones

The source’s intergenerational value V=Σδ^t(Bₜ−Cₜ) is correct, and so is its warning that discounting is an ethical and economic choice, not a physical law. The scale is easy to underestimate. A harm of 1,000,000 units one hundred years away has a present value of about 369,700 at a 1% annual rate, 52,000 at 3%, and 1,150 at 7%. A choice among common rates changes the weight of the distant harm by a factor of more than 300. As Chapter 82 argued, irreversible harms and lost options are better treated as constraints than as discounted costs. The generational transition Xₙ₊₁=T(Xₙ,Aₙ,Eₙ) and the source’s questions about what each generation preserves, changes, risks and leaves open belong with that argument.

The source’s milestone principle is a claim about this book. It says seven hundred principles are a developing structure, a graph G_K=(V,E), not seven hundred independent truths, and that the count establishes neither completeness nor correctness. That is right. Seven hundred items allow 244,650 possible pairwise links, and which of them are real dependencies is the work of the edges, not the count. The source’s distinction between a complete edition and a final one is the stance of this manuscript: a revision is complete and checkable, yet it remains open to correction. Its knowledge update Kₙ₊₁=Kₙ+ΔKₙ+ΔUₙ, where recognized uncertainty is counted as a gain, is conceptual. It matches Chapter 67’s point that well-described uncertainty is part of what is known.

Thesis

Survival and repetition add no truth. Information along a chain of transmission can only decline without new evidence, institutional capacity is limited by its necessary weakest component, error settles where detection balances its arrival, and the weight of the distant future depends on a chosen discount rate.

Then find the steady error stock when c=4 new errors arrive each period and a fraction q=0.2 is corrected. Finally, compute the present value of a harm of 1,000,000 units one hundred years away at annual discount rates of 1% and 7%.

Chapter 31: Shared Failure, Disagreeing Records, and Evidence With Gaps

Two copies that fail together are one copy counted twice.

Principles 945–954 deal with a root of trust and a claim of truth, verifying origins across distributed systems, shared failure in independent networks, evidence when institutions disagree, legitimate reconstruction after loss, recovery and restoration, uncertainty in inherited systems, the limits of historical completeness, provenance during reconstruction, and continuity from incomplete evidence. This chapter adds three calculations: the joint failure of two correlated systems, how a disagreement score depends on the completeness of stated uncertainties, and how far a selectively preserved record can mislead.

Correlated Failure, Quantified

The source gives the joint failure probability of two systems with equal failure probability p and binary failure correlation ρ as P(F₁∩F₂)=p²+ρp(1−p), reducing to p² when independent and to p when perfectly correlated. The formula is correct. It has a direct reading: it is what results if, a fraction ρ of the time, the second system simply shares the first system’s failure process and otherwise fails independently. With p=0.01 the independent pair fails together with probability 0.0001, as the source says. A correlation of only 0.1 raises this to about 0.0011, eleven times higher; a correlation of 0.5 raises it to about 0.005, fifty times higher. Most of the benefit of the second copy is lost at correlations that would be hard to detect in ordinary operation, since joint failures are rare by construction. This is why measured independence, not nominal independence, governs redundancy, and why design diversity is valued and difficult to verify.[55] The source’s qualifications — shared software, suppliers, governance, assumptions and data sources (947) — list the usual causes of such correlation.

Figure 31.1. Left: joint failure probability of two systems with individual failure probability 0.01 as their failure correlation ρ rises from 0 to 1, against the independent value 0.0001. Right: a seeded population of standard-normal values and the 60% that survive when values above zero survive with probability 0.9 and values below zero with probability 0.3; the survivors’ mean is about 0.40 instead of 0. Idealized models.

A Disagreement Score Depends on Its Uncertainties

The source measures disagreement between two institutions’ results x_A±σ_A and x_B±σ_B by z=|x_A−x_B|/√(σ_A²+σ_B²), and says correctly that a large z indicates a difference hard to explain by the stated random uncertainties alone. The score is only as good as those uncertainties. Take 10.0±0.3 and 11.0±0.4: the stated values give z=2.0. If the two results share a calibration and their errors are positively correlated with ρ=0.5, the uncertainty of the difference is √(σ_A²+σ_B²−2ρσ_Aσ_B)≈0.36 and z rises to about 2.8. If instead the second result omits a systematic uncertainty of 0.5, the full denominator is about 0.71 and z falls to about 1.4. The same pair can look like a clear conflict or an unremarkable difference depending on what was left out of the uncertainty budget. Its record D=(C_A,C_B,E_A,E_B,M_A,M_B,U), keeping each claim with its evidence and method, is what allows the budget to be reexamined later (Chapter 71).

Its inverse-variance combination of an inherited value with a new measurement (951) is correct under the stated independence and repeats Chapter 25, which showed how a shared calibration error makes the combined uncertainty misleadingly small, as the source warns. Its rule U_future≥U_known is, as it says, not a mathematical law: new independent evidence can reduce uncertainty. Its intended meaning is better stated as a requirement that the uncertainty a later user states should not be smaller than the evidence supports.

A Record That Survived Selectively

The source says that a record R=P(H) is a partial projection of the history H, that the size of the missing portion is not always known, and that missing data may be systematically different from the surviving data (952). A simple case shows how much this matters. Suppose the original values follow a standard normal distribution, and a value above zero survives with probability 0.9 while a value below zero survives with probability 0.3. Then 60% of the record survives — a fraction that alone looks reassuring — but the surviving mean is about 0.40 standard deviations above the true mean of zero. If the same 60% had survived at random, the surviving mean would be unbiased. The surviving fraction says nothing about which case applies; only knowledge of the loss process does. This is Rubin’s distinction between data missing at random and data missing not at random (Chapter 27). It is why the source’s provenance graph G_P=(V,E) and its recorded transformations (953) matter: they are the only route to knowing how the surviving record was selected.

Thesis

Redundancy fails at correlations too small to observe directly, a disagreement score inherits every omission in its uncertainty budget, and a surviving record can be biased by its losses even when much of it survives.

Then, for results 10.0±0.3 and 11.0±0.4, compute z under independence, with error correlation 0.5, and with an omitted systematic uncertainty of 0.5 in the second result. Finally, for standard-normal values where values above zero survive with probability 0.9 and values below zero with probability 0.3, find the surviving fraction and the surviving mean.
